## Overview

The Chokwe (also *Cokwe*, *Tshokwe*, *Tchokwe*, *Kioko*, *Bajokwe*) are a Bantu-speaking people of south-central Africa whose historic homeland straddles the upper Kasai and Kwango watersheds along what is today the border between the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Angola, and Zambia. Their language, *Cokwe* (Guthrie zone K.11), belongs to the Chokwe–Lucazi cluster of western Bantu and is closely related to Lwena (Luvale), Luchazi and Mbunda; the four together are sometimes treated as a single dialect continuum by ethnographers. Population estimates for the Chokwe proper range from roughly 1.3 to 1.5 million, of whom perhaps half a million live in the DRC's Kasai and Katanga provinces, with the largest concentrations in Angola's Lunda Norte, Lunda Sul and Moxico. Historically the Chokwe originated as small hunter-gatherer and matrilineal chieftaincies on the fringe of the Lunda empire around the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, absorbed Lunda court culture through the *mwanangana* (land-holding chief) institution, and in the second half of the nineteenth century — flush with ivory, beeswax and rubber wealth from long-distance trade with the Ovimbundu and Portuguese — expanded aggressively northward, eventually sacking the Lunda capital *Musumba* around 1885. In folk-culture terms the Chokwe matter as one of the great sculptural traditions of Central Africa: the *chihongo* and *mwana pwo* masks, the caryatid stool and throne-chair (*ngundja*), the divination basket *ngombo ya cisuka*, and the anthropomorphised *hamba* ancestor figures are among the most instantly recognisable objects in the African art canon.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

Chokwe textile art belongs less to loom weaving than to the graphic vocabulary of *sona* — the tradition of ideographic sand-drawings executed on smoothed earth by elders as mnemonics for proverbs, cosmological narratives and initiation lore. The same repertoire of continuous-line lattice patterns migrates onto raffia mats, beaded belts, incised gourds and mask cheeks, and shares a deep structural kinship with the *lusona* drawings of the neighbouring Lwena and Luchazi. Cloth itself was historically raffia palm (*Raphia vinifera*) fibre, woven on a single-heddle horizontal loom into square panels that were pieced together for skirts and overmantles; the surfaces were then embroidered, cut-pile ("Kasai velvet") or painted with red *tukula* (camwood powder) and kaolin. From the nineteenth century onward imported cotton trade cloth largely displaced raffia, but the graphic repertoire persisted. Recurring motifs include *cingelyengelye* (the interlaced cross of the Portuguese Order of Christ, absorbed into Chokwe royal iconography), the concentric-diamond *mikonda*, and knot-motifs (*jinga*) associated with matrilineal continuity.

### Clothing & dress

Traditional male dress centred on a raffia wrap-skirt (*mahamba*) or hide loincloth secured by a wide beaded belt, augmented on ceremonial occasions by a leopard skin (*ngo*) draped over one shoulder — the prerogative of the *mwanangana* — and by a fibre or basketry crown incorporating antelope horns, brass tacks and cowries. The chief's regalia included a distinctive projecting coiffure or wig, the elaborate winged-and-braided form which is stylised in the *mwana pwo* and *chihongo* masks and which appears carved onto the heads of the seated ancestor figures. Women wore a longer wrap tied at the chest or waist, often over a beaded loin-cord (*mikonda*), with heavy anklets, layered bead necklaces and, in some communities, a projecting labret or filed incisors as beauty markers. Body decoration by scarification (*mikonda ya kucisa*) — raised keloid patterns on the abdomen, temples and back, arranged in the same lattice grammar as the *sona* drawings — was until the mid-twentieth century a compulsory correlate of a woman's initiation. Ceremonial male dancers of the *mukanda* circumcision cycle wear knotted-string body-nets and raffia-fibre skirts (*mahezu*) that shake percussively with the drum pulse.

### Architecture

The Chokwe have no monumental stone tradition and their vernacular architecture is a modest one of rectangular pole-and-*dagga* houses with pitched thatch roofs, arranged in dispersed matrilineal hamlets (*cifuci*) around a central plaza that holds the men's shelter (*cota*), the ancestor shrine and, seasonally, the *mukanda* initiation enclosure. The *cota* is the significant built form: an open-sided pavilion of forked posts and a conical or hipped grass roof, its lintels and central king-post often carved with figurative and geometric relief, functioning simultaneously as courthouse, guesthouse and place of male sociability. The *mukanda* itself is a temporary bush camp — a fenced clearing at some distance from the village containing sleeping shelters and a special lodge for the masked spirit-guardians — which is ritually burned at the closure of the initiation cycle. Chiefly compounds were distinguished by a palisade of *mulemba* (ficus) posts and by the placement inside the enclosure of the great seated ancestor figures and the throne-chair itself, rather than by architectural elaboration.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Chokwe pottery is a low-fired, hand-coiled, women's craft producing rounded cooking pots, water jars (*mulondo*) and beer pots (*cizanga*), often with combed or roulette-impressed shoulders and blackened by post-firing smudging in leaves; it is technically accomplished but not the group's signature medium. Blacksmithing, by contrast, was historically prestigious and ritually charged: the *fuli* (smith) produced the crescent-blade axes, throwing knives and ceremonial swords whose forms are echoed in the hands of carved ancestor figures, as well as the iron bells (*mpwevo*) hung on hunting dogs and the chief's staff finials. The great domain, however, is wood-carving. The **Chokwe chair** — a European-derived four-legged high-backed form adopted from Portuguese prototypes in the seventeenth or eighteenth century and utterly transformed — becomes a narrative object: the stretchers and back panels are populated with dozens of miniature carved figures depicting scenes from *mukanda* initiation, hunting, drumming, breastfeeding and copulation, together forming a compressed encyclopaedia of Chokwe social life. The caryatid stool (*ngundja*), the double-headed staff of office (*mwoyo*), the tobacco mortar, the comb (*cisakulu*), the snuff container and above all the standing ancestor figure (*hamba*, plural *mahamba*) — often representing the culture-hero chief *Cibinda Ilunga* with his musket, powder horn and hunter's regalia — share a single sculptural language of massive coiffures, half-closed eyes under a heavy brow, filed teeth and geometrically abstracted torsos. The divination apparatus *ngombo ya cisuka* is a lidded basket packed with sixty-plus miniature figurines, bones, seeds and iron objects (*tuponya*) which the *tahi* diviner casts and reads by the configurations that surface.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Chokwe personal adornment is dense with beadwork, brass and iron. Multi-strand bead collars, waistbeads (*mikonda*), and beaded aprons for young initiates use imported Venetian glass beads traded in from the Atlantic coast, worked in the same lattice patterning as *sona*. Brass and copper anklets and armlets, often heavy spiralled forms, mark rank and marital status; ivory pendants carved as miniature *pwo* faces (*mikisi mihake*) were worn by hunters and diviners as protective amulets. The characteristic keloid scarification of women — *cingelyengelye* over the sternum, radial patterns around the navel, temple bars — is treated in the ethnographic literature as jewellery in its own right, and is faithfully reproduced on the cheeks and forehead of the *mwana pwo* mask. Filed and pointed upper incisors, formerly widespread, are now rare. Men of hunting distinction wore necklaces of leopard claw and warthog tusk; diviners added antelope horns filled with medicinal *malemba*.

## Music & performance

Chokwe music is polyrhythmic and drum-driven, structured around the interlocking of the tall single-headed *cinguvu* drum, the smaller *cizanji* and *pwita* friction drum, iron double-bell (*rubembe*), rattles (*sanji*) and the slit-log signal drum. The melodic voice is carried by the *cisanji* lamellophone (thumb piano) with its characteristic gourd resonator and by the pluriarc *cihumba* (a bow-lute of five strings, each with its own neck), used both for solo praise-singing and for accompanying the *sona* narrator. Solo song genres include *misambo* (praise poems to chiefs and ancestors, elaborately melismatic) and *masumu* (topical and satirical songs performed at drinking parties). All *mukanda* processions are announced by the deep boom of the *cinguvu* answered by the higher patter of hand-drums, and the arrival of the *makishi* masked spirits at the closing ceremony is signalled by a distinctive stop-and-start clave rhythm that the audience recognises without needing to see the maskers.

## Dance & theatre

Chokwe masquerade is properly the theatre of the *makishi* (singular *likishi*) — masked embodiments of ancestral and bush spirits who emerge from the *mukanda* initiation camp and dance for the community at its opening and closing. The repertoire is broad and codified. The male *chihongo* (*cihongo*) mask, a broad disc-faced form with radiating raffia beard and a swept-back crest, represents wealth, chiefly power and the male ancestor and was historically the prerogative of the *mwanangana*. The female *pwo* or *mwana pwo* mask — a serene, finely modelled wooden face with almond eyes, filed teeth, keloid scarification on the temples and cheeks, and an elaborate fibre coiffure — is danced by a man and embodies the archetypal young woman, ancestress and bringer of fertility. Other named characters include the towering conical *chikunza* (patron of the initiates and of hunting), the fringed sun-disc *kalelwa* associated with rain and rites of passage, and the massive net-and-resin *cikungu* mask of the paramount chief, brought out only for the most senior royal occasions. The dance vocabulary combines pelvic isolations, whole-body tremors that make the fibre skirts rustle in polyrhythmic counterpoint to the drums, sudden freezes and stylised mimicry (women pounding, men hunting) that read as a physical commentary on the sung text. The related *Makishi masquerade* of the closely allied Luvale and Chokwe of Zambia's Zambezi region is inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity (2008, originally proclaimed 2005).

## Festivals & rituals

The central ritual complex is *mukanda*, the boys' circumcision and initiation cycle, held every few years for a cohort of eight-to-fifteen-year-olds who are secluded in a bush camp for a period ranging from a few months to more than a year. During seclusion the boys are circumcised, taught the group's esoteric knowledge (mask lore, *sona* drawings, hunting technique, sexual conduct, ancestor genealogy), given new adult names, and progressively introduced to the *makishi*. The cycle closes with the burning of the camp, the public dance of the masks and the reintroduction of the initiates to their mothers, who ritually fail to recognise them. A parallel but shorter and less elaborate female initiation, *mwali* or *ukule*, marks a girl's first menstruation with seclusion, instruction in domestic and sexual life, scarification and a coming-out dance in which she wears the *pwo*-like adornment of the new woman. Ancestor veneration is organised around household and lineage *hamba* figures, which receive offerings of millet beer, tobacco and blood; larger public rituals address the tutelary spirits of hunting (*Cibinda Ilunga*) and of the chieftaincy. Divination sessions using the *ngombo* basket are convened to diagnose illness, sudden death, infertility or theft, and remain widely consulted even in nominally Christian communities.

## Foodways

The Chokwe subsistence base is a shifting-cultivation staple of cassava (*makamba*), supplemented in the wetter zones by maize, millet and sorghum, with peanuts, cowpeas, bambara nuts, sweet potato, pumpkin and leafy greens (*matapa*, cassava leaves pounded with peanut). The daily staple is a stiff porridge (*funji* or *nsima*) of cassava flour, taken with a sauce of pounded leaves, dried fish from the Kasai and its tributaries, smoked bushmeat, or beans. Hunting, historically ideologically central and the domain of the *cibinda* (master-hunter), contributes duiker, bushpig, cane rat and — for chiefs — leopard and elephant. Palm wine tapped from the raffia and oil palms, and a millet or maize beer (*walwa*), lubricate all social occasions; the calabash beer-pot passed around a seated circle is itself a ritual object. Salt was historically produced by evaporation of vegetable ash lyes and traded across the plateau. Cooking is done on three-stone hearths in a separate kitchen shelter behind the main house, and women eat separately from men on most ordinary occasions.

## Oral tradition & literature

Chokwe oral literature is unusually well documented for a Central African group, thanks to twentieth-century collections by Portuguese and Belgian ethnographers (Baumann, Delachaux, Bastin, Redinha). The corpus is dominated by *yishima* (long historical narratives) recounting the migration from *Musumba*, the exploits of *Cibinda Ilunga* the hunter-prince who married the Lunda princess *Lueji* and founded the chiefly lineage, and the nineteenth-century wars of expansion. Around this royal spine cluster genealogical praise-poems (*jinjimbo*) recited by court bards, cautionary animal tales (*yishimo*) featuring the trickster tortoise and hare, riddling contests (*jinongonongo*) exchanged around the evening fire, and the great didactic tradition of *sona* — the ideographic drawings whose execution is accompanied by the singing or reciting of a fixed narrative, so that the graphic form and the verbal text function as a single mnemonic system. Personal names, praise names taken at initiation, and drum-signalled proverbs form a further layer of oral art. The lattice-based *sona* tradition is often mentioned in the same breath as the *lukasa* memory boards of the Luba to the east, though the two systems are formally quite different — *lukasa* being a beaded and pegged wooden tablet, *sona* a continuous line traced in sand.

## Language & religion

*Cokwe* is a Bantu language of Guthrie zone K.11, mutually intelligible in significant measure with Lwena (Luvale), Luchazi and Mbunda; it is a tonal, agglutinative language with the classic Bantu noun-class morphology (some eighteen classes), and is written in a Latin orthography developed by Protestant and Catholic missions in the early twentieth century, with modest but stable print and radio use in both Angola and the DRC. The traditional religious cosmology recognises a distant creator (*Kalunga* or *Nzambi*), a middle stratum of ancestral spirits (*mahamba*) who intervene actively in daily life through dreams, illness and divinatory signs, and a lower stratum of nature-spirits attached to particular rivers, groves and hunting grounds. Ritual specialists include the *tahi* (basket diviner), the *cimbanda* (herbalist-healer), the *fuli* (smith, always ritually significant), and the *mwanangana* (land-chief), who is himself a ritual figure mediating between the ancestors and the living community. From the late nineteenth century Catholic and Protestant missions (notably the Plymouth Brethren in Angola and the Methodists in the DRC) established a substantial Christian presence, and today most Chokwe are nominal Christians who continue nevertheless to consult *ngombo* diviners, participate in *mukanda* and honour *hamba* figures — a syncretism that is standard across the region and that has, if anything, been reinforced by the disruptions of the Angolan civil war and the mass displacement of the 1980s and 1990s.

## Sources & further reading

- Marie-Louise Bastin, *La sculpture Tshokwe* (1982) and *Art décoratif Tshokwe* (1961) — the standard scholarly catalogue of Chokwe visual arts.
- Manuel Jordán (ed.), *Chokwe! Art and Initiation Among Chokwe and Related Peoples* (Prestel, 1998) — exhibition catalogue with essays on masks, initiation and the diaspora.
- José Redinha, *Paredes pintadas da Lunda* and other Companhia de Diamantes de Angola monographs (1950s–60s).
- Paulus Gerdes, *Sona Geometry from Angola: Mathematics of an African Tradition* (2006) — the mathematical structure of *sona* drawings.
- UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage: *Makishi masquerade* (Zambia, inscribed 2008), the closely related Luvale–Chokwe tradition.
- Wikipedia: "Chokwe people", "Chokwe language", "Mwana Pwo", "Cibinda Ilunga", "Makishi masquerade".
- Daniel Biebuyck, *The Arts of Zaire, Volume II* (University of California Press, 1986), chapter on Chokwe and related peoples.
